raw_case_text: In July 2022, a 52-year-old woman was diagnosed with SLE, lupus nephritis, and polyserositis. She presented with symptoms of facial edema, anorexia, nausea, abdominal distention, cough, and white phlegm. The severity of her condition was measured using the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI), which scored 20. Initially, the patient received treatment with glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone, prednisone), immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil), and hydroxychloroquine sulfate. After confirming no contraindications such as infection or allergies, the patient began receiving belimumab (480mg) on July 22, 2022. Four rounds of therapy were completed by September 29, 2022. During this period, the patient's symptoms gradually improved, and her SLEDAI score decreased. As a result, the dosage of glucocorticoids and mycophenolate mofetil was gradually reduced. However, in October, the patient developed an infection with the herpes zoster virus. Although she did not experience a noticeable cough or expectoration, she had occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath. Before the fifth belimumab therapy, on November 1, 2022, a chest computed tomography scan revealed patchy, nodular, and flocculent ground-glass density shadows in all lung lobes, as well as nodules and cavities in the dorsal segment of the left lower lobe. These findings indicated pulmonary infiltration associated with SLE and pulmonary infectious lesions (Figure 1a and b). HIV and anti-IFN-gamma autoantibody test results were negative. White blood count and C-reactive protein were normal. Serum beta-D-glucan, serum galactomannan, cryptococcal capsular antigen, tuberculosis antibody, candida IgG antibody and candida antigen test were negative. CD4+T lymphocyte count was 332/ul (reference range, 180-324/ul), CD8+T lymphocyte count was 646/ul (reference range, 1185-1901/ul), absolute NK cell count was 16/ul (reference range, 200-587/ul), IgG 5.44 g/L (reference range, 8-18g/L), IgA 1.16g/L (reference range, 0.9-4.5g/L), IgM 0.64g/L (reference range, 0.84-1.32g/L). The next generation sequencing (NGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) showed that Pneumocystis jirovecii (sequence number 178940) and Talaromyces marneffei (sequence number 7480). TM was cultured from the patients' BALF (Figure 2a and b). Meanwhile, BALF was positive for PJ by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Finally, we discontinued the fifth belimumab therapy. Voriconazole (0.6g/d on day 1 and 0.4g/d from day 2) was used to treat TM infection. She had a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Therefore, PJ pneumonia was treated with clarithromycin 1.8g/d for the first week. Our test for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase was normal. Clarithromycin was changed to sulfamethoxazole. The treatment of SLE, maintenance of prednisone 5mg/d, MMF 0.75g/d, hydroxychloroquine sulfate 0.2g/d. After about one month of therapy, the reexamination of chest computed tomography showed that the pneumonia was improved (Figure 1c and d). The patient is still under follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old woman with systemic erythematosus (SLE) and lupus nephritis presented with occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath prior to her fifth scheduled dose of belimumab.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In July 2022, the patient was diagnosed with SLE, lupus nephritis, and polyserositis (initial SLEDAI score 20) after presenting with facial edema, anorexia, nausea, abdominal distention, cough, and white phlegm. She was treated with glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone, prednisone), cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), hydroxychloroquine sulfate, and four infusions of intravenous belimumab (480 mg starting July 22, 2022, through September 29, 2022), achieving clinical improvement that allowed tapering of glucocorticoids and MMF. In October 2022, she developed herpes zoster virus infection. Prior to her fifth scheduled belimumab infusion on November 1, 2022, she reported occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath without noticeable cough or expectoration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), lupus nephritis, and polyserositis (diagnosed July 2022); herpes zoster infection (October 2022); reported history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for occasional chest tightness and mild shortness of breath at the November 2022 presentation; negative for noticeable cough or sputum expectoration. Prior July 2022 onset included facial edema, anorexia, nausea, abdominal distention, cough, and white phlegm.

objective.routine_investigations: November 2022 laboratory workup: White blood cell count and C-reactive protein (CRP) normal; HIV antibody negative; anti-IFN-gamma autoantibody negative; serum galactomannan, cryptococcal capsular antigen, tuberculosis antibody, Candida IgG antibody, and Candida antigen tests all negative; quantitative G6PD enzyme activity assay normal. Immunoglobulins: IgG 5.44 g/L (reference range: 8–18 g/L), IgA 1.16 g/L (reference range: 0.9–4.5 g/L), and IgM 0.64 g/L (reference range: 0.84–1.32 g/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (November 1, 2022): Patchy, nodular, and flocculent ground-glass density shadows across all lung lobes, accompanied by nodules and cavities in the dorsal segment of the left lower lobe. Fungal biomarker: Serum beta-D-glucan negative. Lymphocyte subsets: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 332/μL (reference range: 180–324/μL), CD8+ T-lymphocyte count 646/μL (reference range: 1,185–1,901/μL), and absolute NK cell count 16/μL (reference range: 200–587/μL). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) detected Pneumocystis jirovecii (178,940 sequence reads) and Talaromyces marneffei (7,480 sequence reads); BALF PCR was positive for P. jirovecii, and BALF fungal culture grew Talaromyces marneffei.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Co-infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) and pulmonary Talaromyces marneffei infection in an immunosuppressed patient with SLE and lupus nephritis receiving belimumab, glucocorticoids, and mycophenolate mofetil, confirmed by BALF mNGS (178,940 P. jirovecii reads and 7,480 T. marneffei reads), positive BALF P. jirovecii PCR, and positive BALF culture for T. marneffei. Plan and clinical course: The fifth dose of belimumab was discontinued. Voriconazole (0.6 g/day on day 1, then 0.4 g/day from day 2) was initiated for T. marneffei. Due to her reported history of G6PD deficiency, PJP was treated with clarithromycin (1.8 g/day) during the first week and subsequently switched to sulfamethoxazole once repeat G6PD testing returned normal. Maintenance SLE therapy was continued with prednisone 5 mg/day, MMF 0.75 g/day, and hydroxychloroquine sulfate 0.2 g/day. Repeat chest CT after 1 month of therapy demonstrated significant improvement of pneumonia, and she remained stable under outpatient follow-up.
